clue.text: Conceit just devised by Thackeray

definitions.note: describes a work rather than naming it; the novel is Thackeray's best known

parts.note: conceit in the sense of pride in oneself is vanity
just means fair, even-handed

explanation.surface: A clever idea that was simply dreamed up by the Victorian novelist Thackeray.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's 1848 satirical novel takes its title from the town fair in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress.

clue.text: Newman apologized for his

parts.note: Cardinal Newman's spiritual autobiography is Apologia Pro ... Sua, a defence of his own life; the missing Latin word means life

explanation.surface: Cardinal Newman said sorry for something of his own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apologized' misleads: Newman's Apologia was a defence, not an apology, of his life, and the Latin title's missing word is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Newman's Apologia Pro Vita Sua defended his life, the Latin word for life filling the title's gap.

clue.text: F. W. Farrar's housemaster shows Christmas spirit

definitions.meaning: a schoolmaster in Farrar's school story Eric, or Little by Little bears this name
the festive season's cheer, the word sung in carols for Christmas

explanation.surface: A Victorian school-story housemaster displays festive goodwill.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a master in Farrar's school novel is also the French-derived word for the Yuletide season.

clue.text: Puzo's patron

parts.note: Mario Puzo's Mafia novel is named for its protective head of a crime family, a sponsor at a christening

explanation.surface: The sponsor or benefactor of the novelist Mario Puzo.
explanation.definitionFit: Puzo's 1969 novel is titled for the Mafia don who acts as patron, also the sponsor at a baptism.

clue.text: Fence isolating young criminals

parts.note: a fence is a receiver of stolen goods, here Dickens's one who keeps a gang of boy thieves shut away in his den

explanation.surface: A barrier that keeps juvenile offenders apart from others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fence' reads as a barrier; it is a dealer in stolen goods, the villain of Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: In Oliver Twist the receiver of stolen goods trains a gang of boy pickpockets in his hideout.

clue.text: Long title revised for 4's gains

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for the adjective that describes them, as in the set phrase with gains

indicators.note: something revised has been altered and reworked, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lengthy book name was changed to suit the profits of the character at 4.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer at 4 is a fence, whose gains are dishonestly acquired; the definition leans on the stock phrase for such profits.
explanation.definitionFit: Stolen goods a fence profits from are dishonestly obtained, the stock phrase being these kinds of gains.

clue.text: Carlyle's sculptor starts brilliantly on his marble

indicators.note: the starts of the four following words are their opening letters, taken in turn

explanation.surface: The artist who sculpted Carlyle begins his work in marble with flair.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Joseph Edgar Boehm made the seated statue of Thomas Carlyle on the Chelsea Embankment.
explanation.definitionFit: Boehm, a Victorian sculptor, made the famous seated statue of Thomas Carlyle in Chelsea.

clue.text: Confessions of an English one emerged piecemeal (5, )

definitions.text: Confessions of an English one emerged piecemeal

parts.words: Confessions of an English one emerged piecemeal
parts.note: De Quincey's Confessions were first published in instalments in the London Magazine, the title naming a user of a narcotic

explanation.surface: The admissions of an Englishman came out bit by bit.
explanation.definitionFit: De Quincey's Confessions of an English Opium-Eater appeared in parts in a magazine in 1821.

clue.text: Same honour, differently packaged, for Gryll Grange or Northanger Abbey, perhaps (5, )

definitions.text: Gryll Grange or Northanger Abbey, perhaps

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are wrapped up in another arrangement

explanation.surface: Reputation repackaged for a pair of novels named after country houses.
explanation.walkthrough: Gryll Grange is Peacock's novel, Northanger Abbey Austen's; both are named after a country seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Both titles name a stately country residence of the landed gentry, an example of such a building.

clue.text: Aquatic bird, wantonly destroyed, with tragic consequences

definitions.text: Aquatic bird, wantonly destroyed, with tragic consequences

parts.words: Aquatic bird, wantonly destroyed, with tragic consequences
parts.note: in Chekhov's play Treplev shoots a coastal bird for no reason, a symbol of the ruined Nina

explanation.surface: A water bird is killed for no reason, and disaster follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Chekhov's play centres on a needlessly shot coastal bird that foreshadows Nina's ruin and Treplev's suicide.

clue.text: Paul the pointilliste added it to account

definitions.text: Paul the pointilliste added it to account

parts.words: Paul the pointilliste added it to account
parts.note: the dotting painter Paul ... surname is this word followed by AC, the usual short form of account

explanation.surface: The dot-painter Paul tacked this on when reckoning up his bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards: the answer plus AC (account) gives SIGNAC, the pointillist painter Paul Signac.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Signac, the neo-impressionist, has a surname that is this word plus the abbreviation for account.

clue.text: Blondness of fisherman indicated by Ellis Peters

definitions.text: Blondness of fisherman indicated by Ellis Peters

parts.words: Blondness of fisherman indicated by Ellis Peters
parts.note: a Cadfael title read as the fair complexion of the apostle who was a fisherman

explanation.surface: The crime writer Ellis Peters tells us the fisherman was fair-haired.
explanation.walkthrough: Ellis Peters's Cadfael novel is named after the Shrewsbury fair on the saint's feast; read literally it describes the apostle's light colouring.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellis Peters's third Cadfael mystery is set during Shrewsbury's annual fair on the feast of the fisherman apostle.

clue.text: Jim nor mother accept revision by political novelist

indicators.note: a revision reworks text, so the letters of the three words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Neither Jim nor his mother will accept the edits.
explanation.definitionFit: The barrister-author of Rumpole also wrote Paradise Postponed, a novel of postwar British politics.

clue.text: "They were not —— creatures; it was that made them so terrible to Helen " (E. M. Forster)

definitions.text: "They were not —— creatures; it was that made them so terrible to Helen " (E. M. Forster)

parts.words: "They were not —— creatures; it was that made them so terrible to Helen " (E. M. Forster)
parts.note: the goblins of Howards End, heard in Beethoven's Fifth, are described as not hostile or belligerent

explanation.surface: A quotation from Forster's Howards End about goblins that frightened Helen.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's goblins were not hostile or combative, which is why they seemed so menacing to Helen Schlegel.

clue.text: Divides underworld adherents?

definitions.note: verb, cuts apart limb from limb

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and the realm itself
adherents of a body are its members

explanation.surface: Splits the followers of the criminal fraternity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld' suggests gangsters; here it is Dis, the classical god of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut up a body into its limbs is to split it into parts, a forceful synonym.

clue.text: "As a discontented friend, —— - —— with his unkindness?" (Coriolanus)

definitions.text: "As a discontented friend, —— - —— with his unkindness?" (Coriolanus)

parts.words: "As a discontented friend, —— - —— with his unkindness?" (Coriolanus)
parts.note: Menenius asks whether he should return to Coriolanus as a friend wounded by sorrow at his coldness

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Coriolanus about a friend hurt by unkindness.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's compound means struck down by sorrow, describing Menenius rebuffed by the unkind Coriolanus.

clue.text: Architect reportedly increases sales

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the phrase is to be heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: a pedlar who sells more hawks more, here two words run together

explanation.surface: A building designer is said to be boosting the turnover.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicholas Hawksmoor was the English Baroque architect of several London churches.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Hawksmoor, pupil of Wren, designed London churches such as Christ Church, Spitalfields.

clue.text: Muse in opera (Tosca, for example)

indicators.note: the word in signals that the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A source of inspiration in an opera such as Puccini's Tosca.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the nine Muses, Erato presides over lyric and love poetry.

clue.text: First Romantic to send out as authority

indicators.note: the first of the word Romantic is its opening letter

parts.note: to emit is to send out, as with light or heat

explanation.surface: The earliest Romantic poet was dispatched as an official envoy.
explanation.definitionFit: A remit is the scope of a body's authority, its terms of reference.

clue.text: They got off the beaten track for Burney and Bulwer Lytton

definitions.text: They got off the beaten track for Burney and Bulwer Lytton

parts.words: They got off the beaten track for Burney and Bulwer Lytton
parts.note: Fanny Burney's last novel and a Bulwer Lytton title both name roaming figures, plural here

explanation.surface: People strayed from familiar paths in books by Fanny Burney and Bulwer Lytton.
explanation.definitionFit: Roamers who leave the beaten path; Burney's The Wanderer and a Bulwer Lytton work share the title.

explanation.surface: The Victorian novelist Mrs Riddell's high-minded pledge.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte Riddell's novel The Earl's Promise names a British peer ranking above viscount.

clue.text: Italian political novelist may be seen as evil, Italian chemist as vile

definitions.text: Italian political novelist may be seen as evil, Italian chemist as vile

parts.words: Italian political novelist may be seen as evil, Italian chemist as vile
parts.note: Carlo, author of Christ Stopped at Eboli, and Primo, the chemist who survived Auschwitz, share a surname that rearranges into the two unpleasant adjectives quoted

explanation.surface: One Italian writer looks wicked and another looks base.
explanation.walkthrough: Carlo and Primo share the surname, and its four letters can be rearranged into either of the two adjectives named.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlo Levi wrote of political exile; Primo Levi, a chemist, wrote The Periodic Table.

clue.text: Sacred writings put back in a devil's library

indicators.note: put back means the letters are turned round to read the other way
the word in signals letters lying inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Holy texts returned to the shelves of a demon's book collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put back' turns ADEV, found in 'a devil's', into the Hindu scriptures; 'library' completes the picture of books.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vedas are the oldest Hindu scriptures, holy texts in Sanskrit.

clue.text: Innovative composer still going strong, though having lost his head

indicators.note: losing a head means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: someone still going strong still lives

explanation.surface: A pioneering musician who is still active despite going mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost his head' drops L from LIVES. Charles Ives was the experimental American composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Ives, the American modernist, pioneered polytonality and collage in music.

clue.text: Joe's unreal, contorted prose style

indicators.note: contorted means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of Joe's, with its S, used as written

explanation.surface: Joe writes in a twisted, unreal way.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalese is the clichéd, sensational writing style typical of newspapers.

clue.text: Direction taken by Tom's firm friend

definitions.meaning: a point of the compass, where the sun rises
Tom Brown's loyal chum at Rugby in Tom Brown's Schooldays is Harry, known by this surname

explanation.surface: The way Tom's steadfast companion went.
explanation.definitionFit: A compass point, and the surname of Tom Brown's closest schoolfriend in Thomas Hughes's novel.

clue.text: Tedious speaker returns a dram to underworld figure

parts.note: a proser is one who talks dully at length

indicators.note: returns means the following short phrase is turned round

parts.note: a dram of spirits is a nip

explanation.surface: A bore gives back a tot of whisky to a gangster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns A NIP into PINA. Proserpina is the Roman queen of the underworld; 'underworld figure' suggests a mobster.
explanation.definitionFit: Proserpina, Roman form of Persephone, was carried off by Pluto to be queen of the dead.
